title: Your weekly seva
hookLine: choose one small regular service you can actually keep

cards: A big January resolution often goes like this. New shoes, big plans, five mornings a week, and by February the plan has quietly gone. Not from laziness.
The plan was too big to keep. Meanwhile, a neighbor walks the same two blocks every evening, year after year, without any fuss. The small thing, kept, outlasts the big thing, dropped.
Seva works the same way. This week brought an unseen kindness, the shoes, a dish, a tenth, a lesson taught. On the last day of seva week, the question is simple: what will you actually keep?

teach.b: In Sikh life, seva is less about big moments than about rhythm.

Some Sikh families keep the same weekly seva for years: the same Sunday shift in the langar kitchen, the same job cleaning the gurdwara's floors before the week begins, driving the same elderly neighbor to the same appointment.
Nobody's counting. It's just what Sunday is.

A gurdwara itself runs on this. Before anyone arrives, someone has already swept the floor, lit the stoves and set out the plates, and tomorrow someone will do it again. Nobody remembers a single morning.
The mornings add up. A single big act can feed haumai, yesterday's ego: look what I did.

A small act, repeated, gets boring to the ego, and that's the point. Around the hundredth time you wipe the same tables, there's nobody left to impress. There's only the table, and the people who'll eat there.
Make it small, specific and regular. Not help more, but every Thursday I'll take my neighbor's bins out.
Not give back, but the first Sunday of the month I'll cook at the gurdwara, or the food bank, or for the new parents down the hall. You can choose tan, man or dhan: your hands, your mind, your purse.
You can choose something you'll never be thanked for. Just choose something you can keep.
One seva, kept, does more than ten, dropped.

how: Many Sikhs keep a regular seva, such as a weekly shift in the gurdwara langar or cleaning, and families often serve together on the same day each week.

o: a donation made to the gurdwara at festivals
service given freely, as part of spiritual life
a formal vow taken when joining the Khalsa

games.q: what's inside the week — tap the pairs.
p: runs on seva done every day

s: the best seva is one big, memorable act
Sikh life puts rhythm first: small acts, kept for years.
small, repeated seva gets boring to the ego
after the hundredth time, there's nobody left to impress.
a weekly seva has to be done at a gurdwara
it can be a neighbor, a food bank, new parents down the hall: any regular service.

games.q: you want to keep a seva. which plan are you most likely to keep?
o: help more, somehow, whenever you can.
every Thursday, take your neighbor's bins out.
volunteer five days a week starting tomorrow.
games.why: small, specific, regular. one seva, kept, does more than ten, dropped.

practice: Let the week's sevas pass in front of you, the unseen kindness, the shoes, the dish, the tenth, the thing you taught, and pick the one that felt most like you.
Make it small enough to keep every week, give it a day and a time, and picture yourself still doing it in six months, when nobody remembers you started. If you pray, you can offer it.

wordCard.voice: Seva. One small, regular service, chosen to be kept, which does its quiet work over months and years.

orig.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi script: service, the path's very first word.

carryVoice: Your line: one seva, kept. Seva week ends here; tomorrow, kirtan begins.
